question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [European motivations for Eastern trade and their geographic context]
options: Constantinople (Istanbul) — City whose fall to the Ottomans in 1453 disrupted the overland spice trade routes to Europe
Alexandria — Egyptian port through which much of the Eastern spice trade reached the Mediterranean
Venice — Italian city-state that dominated the Mediterranean spice trade before the Portuguese sea route was found
Antwerp — Portuguese spice distribution hub in northern Europe that the English EIC directly replaced after 1600
wrong_fact: The English EIC did NOT directly replace Antwerp as a Portuguese spice hub. Antwerp was the main distribution centre for Portuguese spices in northern Europe in the early 1500s, but by 1600 Antwerp had declined (sacked 1576, taken by Spain 1585). The EIC's rise was more a response to the Dutch-dominated spice trade of Amsterdam, not a direct replacement of Antwerp.
explanation: The fall of Constantinople in 1453 blocked traditional overland routes, pushing Europeans to seek sea routes. Venice dominated Mediterranean spice trade. Alexandria was a key transit port for Eastern goods. Antwerp was the Portuguese distribution hub in northern Europe in the early 16th century, but had declined by 1600 when the EIC was formed — the EIC competed primarily with the Dutch VOC, not directly replacing Antwerp.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Key events in the historical background of the English EIC and their locations]
options: Calicut — Port where Vasco da Gama landed in 1498, opening the sea route from Europe to India
Tordesillas — Spanish town where the 1494 treaty divided the world between Spain and Portugal, excluding England
Azores — Portuguese Atlantic islands used as a staging point for voyages around Africa
Hormuz — Island fortress where the English explorer John Cabot first challenged Portuguese power in Asia
wrong_fact: John Cabot did NOT challenge Portuguese power at Hormuz. John Cabot (Giovanni Caboto) sailed for England in 1497 and reached the coast of North America (Newfoundland). He never went to Hormuz in the Persian Gulf. It was later English forces (under Robert Sherley and EIC ships) that clashed with the Portuguese at Hormuz in 1622.
explanation: Vasco da Gama's 1498 landing at Calicut opened the Indian Ocean sea route. The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) gave Portugal dominance east of its meridian, shutting out England legally. The Azores were a key Portuguese Atlantic waypoint. John Cabot sailed to North America for England in 1497 — Hormuz was taken from the Portuguese by Shah Abbas of Persia with English EIC naval assistance in 1622.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Geographic milestones in European exploration that provided context for the EIC's founding]
options: Bartholomeu Dias — Cape of Good Hope (1488) — First European to round the southern tip of Africa
Vasco da Gama — Calicut/Kozhikode (1498) — First European to reach India by sea, opening the eastern spice route
Francis Drake — Straits of Magellan and Pacific (1578) — First Englishman to circumnavigate the globe
Walter Raleigh — Spice Islands / Maluku (1595) — First English voyage to the East Indies, preceding the EIC's first official voyage
wrong_fact: Walter Raleigh did NOT voyage to the Spice Islands in 1595. Raleigh's 1595 expedition went to the Orinoco River in South America (in search of El Dorado). The first English voyage to the East Indies before the EIC was the Cumberland/Lancaster Levant Company expeditions and James Lancaster's pre-EIC voyage of 1591–94. Raleigh had no connection with the Maluku (Spice Islands).
explanation: Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488. Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498. Francis Drake completed the first English circumnavigation (1577–1580), passing through the Strait of Magellan. Walter Raleigh is associated with Virginia (1585) and the Orinoco expedition (1595), not the East Indies. The first pre-EIC English voyage to the East Indies was James Lancaster's (1591–1594).
